slides.notes: Point back to the golden-thread slide from the front section and land on the Day 2 row. Say the deliverable out loud: real tools behind real authorisation, plus memory that survives a session without leaking across customers. Yesterday's agent could think; today it can act and remember — and both of those are attack surfaces, which is why Module 3 starts with authorisation, not APIs.

slides.title: Tool use, function calling and MCP
slides.subtitle: The difference between an agent that talks about your order and one that finds it.
items: Function-calling contract
Narrow, typed tools
Four trust boundaries
Server-side authorisation
slides.notes: This module turns yesterday's empty state machine into something that touches Tawseel's real order, logistics and billing systems. Say plainly: the hardest idea today is not the API wrapping, it is where authorisation lives — that single question runs through every slide and resurfaces in Module 8. No memory yet; that is this afternoon.

slides.title: Rafeeq needs real systems, not prose
slides.intro: Every enterprise agent eventually has to touch systems it does not own — and that ownership boundary is where the engineering gets hard.

bullets.text: Tawseel's order-management (Java), logistics tracker (Go) and CRM (SaaS) are owned by three teams with three auth models.
Exposes 'get account balance' and 'raise dispute' as MCP tools behind existing auth; many agents reuse them without touching core banking.
Citizen-service actions become MCP tools with per-tool authorisation, so an agent's blast radius equals exactly what it was granted.
That is the current cost of a bespoke integration plus security review — and leadership wants two more agents next quarter.
MCP turns each system into a governed, discoverable tool server — published once, consumed by every agent that follows.

aside.title: WHERE THIS BITES
aside.body: Hard-wiring an agent to each backend's own SDK is a maintenance and security nightmare — a schema change in one system becomes a silent break in every agent that imported it directly.

slides.notes: Ask the room: how many backend systems would your own org's support agent need to touch? Most will say three to six. That number is exactly why one server per backend, not one giant integration, is this module's answer. Keep this to four minutes.

slides.title: The function-calling round trip
slides.caption: The model never runs code — it requests a call; the runtime decides whether and how to honour it. That separation is the first security boundary, deepened in Module 8.
slides.notes: Draw this as a sequence on the board before revealing: model, runtime, tool, observation, model. Stress the word 'requests' — say it twice. The whole module's authorisation argument follows from this one fact: the model asks, it does not act, so something else must decide, and that something is the runtime, never the prompt.

slides.title: Function calling: a structured contract

bullets.text: The developer describes each tool as name, description and JSON-schema parameters — the whole contract, nothing implicit.
The model emits a structured call request instead of answering; the runtime decides whether to honour it.
The model never runs code itself — that separation is the first security boundary, deepened in Module 8.
An LLM uses a tool exactly as well as its description and parameter names let it — nothing more, nothing hidden.

slides.notes: Say 'the schema is the prompt' slowly — it is the module's most quoted line and the reason the next slide exists. Ask the room to name a tool they have used that had a one-word description; someone always has a war story about the model misusing it.

slides.title: Tool design: narrow beats mega

left.title: Mega-tool
left.subtitle: logistics(action, **kwargs)
items: One entry point for every operation — the model must guess the right action string.
Returns whatever the raw backend gives back — an unbounded blob.
A docstring that says 'does logistics stuff' teaches the model nothing.

right.title: Four narrow tools
right.subtitle: track_shipment, estimate_eta, ...
items: One tool, one job — the model routes to the right one far more reliably.
Typed, compact output: status, ETA, SLA flag — not the backend's own shape.
Docstring states what it does, when to use it, when NOT to, and the id format.

slides.notes: This is mistake #1 from the module's own list, made concrete before you reach the mistakes slide. Read track_shipment's real docstring aloud from tools/tawseel.py later this module and ask the room to compare it against the left column's one-liner — the gap is the whole argument for narrow tools.

slides.title: What MCP decouples
slides.intro: An open, JSON-RPC standard for exposing tools, resources and prompts — not this course's invention.

bullets.text: An MCP server exposes capabilities; the agent's MCP client discovers and calls them at runtime — no hard-coded list.
The agent depends on the protocol, not each backend's SDK. Swap the logistics backend and the tool contract is unchanged.
A capability is published once and consumed by many agents, with one place to authorise, rate-limit and audit.
The Model Context Protocol specification defines what MCP guarantees — not a tutorial's simplification of it.

aside.title: MENTAL MODEL
aside.body: MCP is to agent tools what a service mesh or API gateway is to microservices — a standard seam for capability, security and observability.

slides.notes: Name the specification explicitly — modelcontextprotocol.io — and say this course's own docs/MCP_TOPOLOGY.md traces every claim back to it, not to a blog post's simplification. If anyone has read a third-party MCP tutorial, ask what it got wrong about authorisation; most skip it entirely, which is exactly this module's complaint.

slides.title: Adapting a real API into a governed tool
slides.intro: Real enterprise APIs are rarely LLM-ready — an adapter sits between MCP and the backend.

bullets.text: Expose 3-4 governed tools, not the backend's 40 endpoints.
Map messy backend responses to the compact typed output the model needs; localise Arabic status strings.
The MCP server checks that THIS agent may call THIS tool for THIS customer — the agent cannot grant itself access.
Rate limits, argument validation and a per-call audit log live in the server, not scattered across agents.

slides.notes: This is the same adapter discipline as Module 1's clean architecture, applied one layer out. Preview that 'enforce authorisation at the server' is not a suggestion in this repo — it is a decorator every one of the four servers shares, coming up in the code slides.

slides.title: Four MCP servers, one trust boundary each
slides.caption: One server per backend, not one mega-server — a review of 'can partner_agent reach billing' becomes a one-line policy check, not an audit of a mega-server's whole surface.
slides.notes: This is the module's anchor diagram — come back to it before the trust-boundary table. Point out the colour shift left to right: orders is calm, billing and customer are hot. Ask the room to guess, before the next slide, which server a compromised agent could do the LEAST damage through.

slides.title: Where should the trust boundary be?
rows: Over-read only — cannot change or delete an order
Can move a delivery time; never touches money or PII
Only server that can move real money — 500 SAR gate enforced twice
Even a jailbroken agent cannot reach another customer's record
slides.footnote: docs/MCP_TOPOLOGY.md and mcp_servers/README.md — this repo's real trust-boundary table, not an illustrative sketch.
slides.notes: This is the course's answer to 'where should the trust boundary be?' — facilitate it as a discussion, do not just read the table. Ask: if Tawseel added a fifth backend tomorrow, own server or fold into orders_server.py? What changes about the review and who signs off, either way? Eight minutes, cap it.

slides.title: The LaDe-shaped operational tool set

cards.title: get_delivery_status
cards.body: Aliased as track_shipment — current status, ETA, SLA flag for one order.

cards.title: get_driver_status
cards.body: A courier's last known activity — internal ops only, never for a customer's 'where is my order'.

cards.title: estimate_eta
cards.body: Current estimated or actual arrival time — never used to promise a NEW delivery time.

cards.title: get_delivery_events
cards.body: The full LaDe-shaped event timeline — accepted through delivered — for disputes and complaints.

cards.title: find_delivery_exception
cards.body: Why a delivery failed: customer_unreachable, damaged, weather — before deciding next steps.

cards.title: Honest sourcing
cards.body: Shaped after LaDe (~10.7M packages, 21k couriers, 5 cities) — we do not redistribute LaDe; this course ships synthetic Saudi data derived from its schema shape.

slides.notes: These five names are lifted straight from LaDe's own tool surface, deliberately — say so. Read the sixth card word for word: this is a licensing and academic-integrity point as much as an engineering one, and participants should be able to defend it if asked in a review.

slides.title: Read tools vs write tools

left.title: Read — idempotent
left.subtitle: track_shipment, get_invoice, ...
items: Safe to retry automatically — Module 9's retry policy keys off IDEMPOTENT.
12 of 16 tools in the governed catalogue.
A transient failure just tries again; nothing changed by the first attempt.

right.title: Write — never blind-retried
right.subtitle: reschedule_delivery, issue_refund, ...
items: A second call can genuinely change state twice — never retried automatically.
issue_refund needs a STABLE idempotency_key per decision, never a fresh one per retry.
registry.py derives WRITE_TOOLS once; nothing else hand-rolls the split.

slides.notes: Point at 'a fresh idempotency key per retry defeats the whole protection' — that is the exact double-refund bug from Module 1, reborn at the tool layer, if a pair gets this wrong in Lab 3. Ask: what does the SAME key on a second call actually do? Answer: replays the original result, never a second payment.

slides.title: Defence in depth: the 500 SAR gate, twice
slides.intro: SPEC's action-risk matrix makes refunds above 500 SAR human-approval-required, not autonomous — enforced in two independent places.

bullets.text: flows/refund_flow.py checks the amount against REFUND_LIMIT_SAR before ever calling the tool.
billing_server.py's issue_refund hard-blocks anything over 500 SAR unless approved=True — no prompt can set that flag for itself.
For an unapproved large refund to go through, both the flow's check AND the server's check would have to be wrong at once.
issue_refund_impl only enforces backend invariants — cannot refund more than was paid — not the 500 SAR policy threshold.

slides.notes: This previews Module 8's defence-in-depth idea one module early — flag that explicitly. Ask: why not just one gate, well-tested? Because a single control that fails silently is a single point of failure; two independent controls is what 'defence in depth' actually means in code, not just in a slide.

slides.title: Curate a CRM tool surface
slides.intro: No lecture — groups pick 3-4 tools from a 20-endpoint CRM API list and justify what they excluded.
bullets: open_case(customer_id, reason) — the one write; mark it non-idempotent.

bullets.text: Defend, out loud, which endpoints did NOT make the cut, and why a wide surface is a liability, not a feature.

slides.notes: Run this in pairs against a printed or projected 20-endpoint CRM list. The teachable moment is always the same: someone wants to include 'update_customer_email' because it exists, and the room has to argue them out of it. Ten minutes, then two groups read their exclusions aloud.

slides.title: A well-designed tool: schema is the prompt

callouts.text: The docstring states what it does, when to use it, when NOT to, and the exact id format — the whole contract.
invalid_order_id_format / order_not_found are returned, never raised — the agent reacts instead of crashing.
ShipmentStatus returns status/eta/SLA flag only — never the backend's own raw blob.

slides.notes: This is the real file, trimmed only for the slide. Read the docstring aloud, then ask: which sentence in it would a vague tool be missing? Every hand should go up for 'do NOT use for refunds' — that line alone prevents a whole class of misrouting.

slides.title: Authorisation enforced at the server

callouts.text: agent_may_access runs BEFORE func(*args) — a denial never reaches the backend adapter.
All four servers share this one decorator — nothing re-derives authorisation by hand.
Success or denial, an audit record is written — the trust-boundary table depends on this line existing.

slides.notes: Point out this is the SAME function wrapping all sixteen tools across all four servers — nobody hand-rolls authorisation per tool. Ask what happens if a tool function itself raises: the try/except one line up (elided here) catches it and still returns an error value, never crashing the server process.

slides.title: The policy table a prompt cannot argue with

callouts.text: change_customer_identity, override_fraud_flag, delete_order — denied before the domain check even runs.
partner_agent gets logistics only, read-only — the classroom answer to 'how narrow is narrow enough'.
Every guarded_tool call goes through agent_may_access — not a prompt, not the agent's own judgement.

slides.notes: Run explain('partner_agent', 'issue_refund', 'CUST-4471') live if you can — it prints reason='domain_not_granted', not a bare False. That reason string is why this module can say authorisation is debuggable, not just enforced.

slides.statement: A prompt is not an access-control mechanism.
slides.statement_ar: التعليمات في الطلب ليست آلية تحكّم في الصلاحيات.
slides.notes: Say it, pause, let it land — same rhythm as every module statement this week. This is the line that resurfaces verbatim in Module 8's guardrail work and in the capstone's DECISIONS.md; tell the room to remember the exact wording, not a paraphrase.

slides.title: Six mistakes that break the tool layer

bullets.text: The model misroutes constantly; split into narrow tools.
'Does order stuff' — the model calls the wrong tool or hallucinates arguments.
Context bloat, cost, and accidental PII exposure.
The loop dies on the first bad id.
The double-refund incident, reborn at the tool layer.
'Only refund if allowed' — a crafted input talks the model past it every time.

slides.notes: Each of these is deliberately reproducible in this repo's sim branches — say so. Have the room match mistake 6 to the exact injected instruction in data/orders/INJECTION_NOTES.md before you move to the case study; it is the sharpest example of the six.

slides.title: Case study: unifying three systems behind MCP
slides.scenario: Tawseel's order-management (Java), logistics-tracking (Go) and CRM (SaaS) are owned by three teams with three auth models. The support-agent project needs all three, and two more agents are planned for next quarter. Each bespoke integration currently takes roughly six weeks and a security review.
slides.challenge: Provide governed, reusable access to all three systems such that a new agent can consume any capability in days, with one authorisation and audit model — while each backend keeps its own auth, PDPL requires per-customer access control, no backend team will rewrite its API, and Arabic status strings must be localised correctly.
slides.solution: Stand up one MCP server per system, each wrapping the backend behind a curated 2-4 tool surface with an adapter that trims outputs and localises. Centralise authorisation and audit in a thin MCP gateway all agents traverse. The customer agent, the ops agent and a partner agent all consume the same servers; adding an agent means granting tool scopes, not building integrations.
questions: Why is 'one MCP server per system' better than 'one big server'?
Where does per-customer authorisation live, and why not in the agent?
How does MCP change the security-review unit from 'per integration' to 'per capability'?
What breaks if a backend team changes a response shape, and how does the adapter contain it?
slides.notes: Facilitate, do not lecture — this is the module's real architecture, not a hypothetical. Push on question 4 especially: the adapter absorbing a field-name change while an unadapted tool breaks is the concrete version of 'the agent depends on the protocol, not the SDK'. Ten minutes, cap it.

slides.title: Five-question recap

bullets.text: What does MCP decouple? The agent from each backend's SDK and contract.
Should a tool raise or return on bad input? Return an error value.
Where must authorisation be enforced? The tool server, never the prompt.
Why must write tools be marked non-idempotent? To prevent blind retries and double actions.
Why four servers, not one mega-server? Independent trust boundaries — review, blast radius and ownership shrink to one domain at a time.

slides.notes: Cold-call style, same as Day 1's recaps. If Q5 gets a shaky answer, point back at the trust-boundary table slide and re-read the billing_server row aloud — that row alone carries most of the argument.

slides.title: Memory and state management
slides.subtitle: Two memories, two jobs — and the PDPL discipline that keeps recall from becoming a data breach.
items: Thread scope
Scoped recall
Versioned KB
PDPL erasure
slides.notes: Say plainly that this module is where Module 3's server discipline meets data governance: memory is the one part of the system where 'it worked' and 'it leaked' can look identical until a customer complains. Ninety minutes, one lab — pace accordingly.

slides.title: Memory turns a novelty into a service
slides.intro: Memory carries the heaviest compliance weight in the whole system — it IS personal-data storage under PDPL.

bullets.text: Rafeeq recalls yesterday's open case and continues rather than restarting.
Retrieves the customer's prior disputes to avoid re-litigating a settled one.
Grounds answers in a retrievable, versioned KB so a change propagates instantly, with no retraining.
Long-term memory IS personal-data storage under PDPL — retention limits, access control, the right to erasure.

aside.title: THE STAKES
aside.body: An agent's memory design is simultaneously a UX feature, a correctness control, and a data-governance surface. Get scoping wrong and 'it remembered' becomes a reportable incident.

slides.notes: Ask the room: has anyone's org shipped a 'personalised' agent where nobody could say exactly what it stored or for how long? That gap is this module's whole argument. Four minutes, then straight into the two-memories split.

slides.title: Two memories, two jobs

cards.label: ST
cards.title: Short-term (working)
cards.body: Scope: one task/thread. Lifetime: the conversation. Backed by a checkpointer. Rafeeq: the current ticket's state — order id found, plan, steps taken.

cards.label: LT
cards.title: Long-term (durable)
cards.body: Scope: across sessions and customers. Lifetime: persistent. Backed by a vector store plus metadata. Rafeeq: customer history, resolutions, policy KB.

cards.title: The classic mistake
cards.body: Stuffing everything into prompt history forever (context overflow), or writing transient task state into long-term storage (noise).

slides.notes: The Module-1 state object IS short-term memory — say that connection explicitly, it is not a new concept, just a persisted one. The rule to write on the board: short-term is the working set for now; long-term is what deserves to outlive the task.

slides.title: Checkpointing: what it buys you
slides.caption: thread_id = "{customer_id}:{channel}:{session_date}" — one customer, one channel, a fresh thread each day so durable facts don't quietly pile up in short-term state.
slides.notes: Walk each of the four boxes with a concrete Rafeeq example: resume after a crash mid-refund, pause before a 600 SAR refund for approval, replay a disputed transition for an auditor, and a customer's second message that day resolving 'it' without repeating the order id.

slides.title: Long-term memory: filter before you rank
slides.intro: Retrieval, not accumulation — embed the situation, find the few most relevant memories, inject only those.

bullets.text: Each memory stores an embedding plus customer_id, type, created_at, locale, policy_version.
Metadata filtering happens before similarity search runs, not after — a PDPL control, not an optimisation.
Durable, reusable facts — resolved-case summaries, stable preferences, policy documents. Not raw messages.
Cap the retrieved items; an SLA policy from last year is worse than no policy at all.

slides.notes: This is the module's central lesson — say the key bullet twice, once fast and once slow. Ask: what would 'filter after rank' actually do wrong? Answer, coming on the retrieval-pipeline slide: an over-broad top-k can leak through before it is trimmed.

slides.title: The retrieval pipeline, filter emphasised
slides.caption: Filtering AFTER ranking can let an over-broad top-k leak through before it is trimmed. Filtering FIRST makes scoping a structural guarantee, not a hope.
slides.notes: Draw a red X over a 'rank then filter' arrow on the board before revealing this slide's correct order. This diagram is the direct ancestor of the leakage test in Lab 4 — say that connection explicitly so the lab does not feel like a new topic.

slides.title: The stale-policy failure, made concrete
rows: Ranks fine on similarity — quotes the WRONG number
Only surfaces if policy_version is filtered first
slides.footnote: The repo genuinely ships both: data/policies/superseded/{en,ar}/refund_eligibility.md exists so this failure is reproducible against real documents, not a hand-built fixture.
slides.notes: This is not an illustrative round number — 300 SAR and 500 SAR are the actual thresholds in this repo's two policy versions. Run policy_context_including_superseded live if you can and let the room watch the 300 SAR chunk outrank the correct one on raw similarity.

slides.title: Cross-lingual retrieval is not optional
slides.intro: Arabic and English memories must be retrievable across languages — a customer asks in Arabic about a note written in English.

bullets.text: An Arabic ticket embeds nowhere near its English-language policy chunk — retrieval returns nothing, or the wrong thing.
HashingEmbeddings in labs, a real multilingual model in production — bridges the AR-EN vocabulary by construction.
Seed at least one customer whose Arabic memory must be retrieved by an English query — do not assume it works.
At least 90% correct policy for AR and EN queries — measured, not assumed.

slides.notes: Ask who in the room has shipped a 'multilingual' RAG system that was quietly English-only underneath. This is common enough that someone usually has a story. The fix is not a bigger model — it is testing the cross-lingual path as its own eval row, not hoping it works.

slides.title: PDPL erasure: forget_customer
slides.intro: A partial erasure is not an erasure from the customer's point of view.

bullets.text: Every one of a customer's embeddings, removed by a real delete on the customer_id filter — never a rank-time exclusion.
forget_customer also erases short-term checkpointed threads by thread_id prefix — half an erasure is not compliance.
Returns an audit-friendly summary — vectors_removed, checkpoints_removed, erased_at — not a bare None.
100% of a customer's data removed — the erasure-completeness target this module is graded against.

slides.notes: Read the phrase 'half an erasure is not a real erasure from the customer's point of view' aloud — it is the module's second most quoted line after the statement slide. Ask why checkpoints need their own erasure path at all, given they are 'just' short-term: because short-term still means personal data at rest.

slides.title: Two collections, two governance regimes

cards.label: PII
cards.title: rafeeq_customer_memory
cards.body: Customer history and resolutions — personal data. Scoped by customer_id on every read. Erasable.

cards.label: KB
cards.title: tawseel_policies
cards.body: Policy documents — not personal data. Versioned, not customer-scoped. Never erased on a customer's request.

cards.title: Never conflate them
cards.body: Separating collections is what lets governance differ: retention, access and erasure apply to one and not the other.

slides.notes: Ask why the policy KB is versioned but the customer-memory collection is not — because policies change on a release cadence the whole company shares, while a customer's memory changes one erasure request at a time. Different axes, different mechanisms, on purpose.

slides.title: Remember or forget?

left.title: Long-term: durable
items: A resolved-case summary, written deliberately.
A stable customer preference (preferred locale, delivery instructions).
A versioned policy chunk.

right.title: Never store
items: An unmasked national id or full card number.
A raw message dump, verbatim.
A transient tool output that has no reuse value.

slides.notes: This compresses the package's fourteen-card sort into the two clearest bins. Run it as a quick show of hands per item rather than a full sort if short on time. The hard middle case worth raising: a customer's stated delivery preference in Arabic — long-term, but still personal data that needs an owner and a retention period.

slides.title: Short-term memory: the checkpointer
slides.code:
def thread_id_for(customer_id: str, channel: str = "app",
                   session_date: str | None = None) -> str:
    """"{customer_id}:{channel}:{session_date}" -- one customer,
    one channel, a FRESH thread each day."""
    if session_date is None:
        session_date = datetime.now(timezone.utc).date().isoformat()
    return f"{customer_id}:{channel}:{session_date}"

def handle_turn(customer_msg: str, thread_id: str,
                 customer_id: str, locale: str = "ar") -> str:
    """A LATER call with the SAME thread_id resumes the checkpointed
    state -- no need to re-send the whole conversation as history."""
    agent = get_checkpointed_agent()
    cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}}  # short-term scope
    out = agent.invoke(
        {"messages": [("user", customer_msg)],
         "customer_id": customer_id, "locale": locale}, config=cfg)
    return out["messages"][-1].content

callouts.text: thread_id_for builds a fresh thread per customer per channel per day — durable facts stay out of it, by construction.
get_checkpointed_agent() is built once per process — resuming a thread_id needs the SAME compiled graph, not a new one.
The checkpoint IS the history; handle_turn only ever sends the new message.

slides.notes: Point at the thread_id format on the board before revealing the function — customer, channel, date, in that order. Ask: what happens if a caller passes a random UUID instead of following the convention? Nothing breaks, but the durable-vs-transient discipline is now the caller's problem, not the system's.

slides.title: Long-term memory: scoped semantic store
slides.code:
def recall(customer_id: str, situation: str, k: int = 3) -> list[str]:
    """THIS customer's memories -- filtered BEFORE ranked. Cross-
    lingual by construction (multilingual embeddings)."""
    store = _customer_store()
    hits = store.similarity_search(
        situation, k=k, filter={"customer_id": customer_id})
    return [h.page_content for h in hits]

def forget_customer(customer_id: str,
                     also_checkpoints: bool = True) -> dict:
    """PDPL erasure: vectors AND, by default, checkpointed threads.
    A vectors-only 'forget' is not a real erasure."""
    store = _customer_store()
    vectors_removed = store.delete(filter={"customer_id": customer_id})
    checkpoints_removed = 0
    if also_checkpoints:
        checkpoints_removed = _erase_checkpoints_for_customer(customer_id)
    return {"customer_id": customer_id,
            "vectors_removed": vectors_removed,
            "checkpoints_removed": checkpoints_removed,
            "vectors_remaining": count_customer_memories(customer_id)}

callouts.text: filter={'customer_id': ...} is passed INTO similarity_search, never applied after — this is the leakage fix.
forget_customer touches both stores — an erasure request spans short-term and long-term memory.
vectors_remaining lets the erasure test assert zero — completeness, checked, not assumed.

slides.notes: This is the file the leakage test in Lab 4 is really about. Trace the filter argument with your finger from recall's call site into similarity_search — it never gets applied after the fact, anywhere in this file. That is the whole PDPL argument in one code path.

slides.title: Grounding in a versioned policy KB
slides.code:
CURRENT_POLICY_VERSION = "2026.2"   # from core/config.py

def policy_context(question: str, locale: str, k: int = 3) -> str:
    """Retrieve the CURRENT version ONLY, filtered BEFORE ranking.
    Refuses to surface SUPERSEDED_POLICY_VERSION under any
    circumstance."""
    hits = _kb_store().similarity_search(question, k=k, filter={
        "policy_version": CURRENT_POLICY_VERSION, "locale": locale,
    })
    return "\n\n".join(h.page_content for h in hits) or "NO_POLICY_FOUND"

def policy_context_including_superseded(question, locale, k=3):
    """DEMO/TEST ONLY: deliberately skips the version filter so the
    stale-memory failure is reproducible. Never called from a normal
    answer path."""
    hits = _kb_store().similarity_search_with_score(
        question, k=k, filter={"locale": locale})
    return [{"content": d.page_content, "score": s} for d, s in hits]

callouts.text: policy_version == CURRENT_POLICY_VERSION is in the filter, not a post-hoc check on the top hit.
NO_POLICY_FOUND — errors as return values, applied to retrieval, exactly like Module 3's tools.

callouts.lead: The demo function exists on purpose
callouts.text: policy_context_including_superseded is how the 300 SAR failure is shown live, never how Rafeeq actually answers.

slides.notes: Point out this file's two functions have opposite jobs by design: one is production, one exists only to make the failure demonstrable. Run both live on the same Arabic refund question if time allows — the contrast is the whole module's argument in thirty seconds.

slides.statement: A filter is a privacy control, not an optimisation.
slides.statement_ar: التصفية آلية لحماية الخصوصية، لا مجرد تحسين للأداء.
slides.notes: Say it, pause, let it land — same rhythm as every module statement. Tie it back explicitly to M3's statement: authorisation lives in the server; scoping lives in the filter. Two different mechanisms enforcing the same idea — a boundary a prompt cannot be trusted to hold.

slides.title: Six mistakes that corrupt memory silently

bullets.lead: 1. Whole history in the prompt, forever.
bullets.text: Context overflow and runaway cost.
Retrieving another customer's memory because it was semantically similar — a PDPL breach.

bullets.lead: 3. Raw messages and PII in the store.
bullets.text: No retention path, no erasure path.
Diluting the signal and paying for tokens that mislead.
The stale-policy failure — 300 SAR quoted as current when it is not.
Embeddings and vector queries have latency and cost that belong in the Module 9 budget.

slides.notes: Mistake 2 is the one Lab 4's leakage test exists entirely to catch — say that directly before moving on. Ask the room to predict, before the case study reveals it, roughly how long a real cross-customer leak like this typically runs before a customer complaint surfaces it.

slides.title: Case study: the cross-customer memory leak
slides.scenario: A retailer's support agent used one vector store, top-5 retrieval, no metadata filter. During a refund conversation it retrieved a different customer's semantically similar note and surfaced their order number and partial address. Roughly 25,000 conversations a day; the leak surfaced only via a customer complaint two weeks in.
slides.challenge: Contain the leak, prove no systemic exposure, and re-architect memory so cross-customer retrieval is impossible, not merely unlikely — without taking the agent offline, while producing an erasure capability for affected customers within days, with Arabic and English notes coexisting.
slides.solution: Enforce customer_id metadata filtering on every read, filter before rank. Split PII-bearing customer memory from the non-personal KB into separate collections with separate governance. Add an erasure path covering vectors and checkpoints. Add a standing leakage test to CI. Stop storing raw messages — store reviewed case summaries only.
questions: Why is metadata filtering a SECURITY control, not an optimisation?
How do you erase a customer across both short-term checkpoints and long-term vectors?
What belongs in a durable case summary vs what must never be stored?
How would you continuously prove non-leakage in production, not just at launch?
slides.notes: Under PDPL this is a reportable personal-data incident, not just a bug — say that plainly before the discussion starts. Push on question 4: a leakage test that only runs once at launch is not a control, it is a snapshot; it has to live in CI, the way this repo's own suite does.

slides.title: Five-question recap

bullets.text: Short-term vs long-term in one line each? The working set for now vs what deserves to outlive the task.
Three properties checkpointing buys you? Resume, human-in-the-loop, audit and time-travel.
Why filter by metadata BEFORE ranking? Correctness and PDPL scoping — a structural guarantee, not a hope.
Why is a superseded policy worse than no policy? Confident, silent wrongness — no exception, no crash.
What does PDPL erasure require of a vector store? A delete path removing the customer's vectors AND checkpoints, verified to zero.

slides.title: Day 2 in one line
points: Tools are an API-design problem for a confused reader — narrow, typed, errors as values, the docstring IS the prompt.
MCP decouples the agent from the backend; four servers make trust boundaries a place you can point at, not a hope.
A prompt is not an access-control mechanism — authorisation lives at the server, in code, every time.
Short-term memory resumes a conversation; long-term memory is data governance — a filter is a privacy control.
